title: Simple motifs in his writing and the influence of Jackie McLean and Andrew Hill
summary: Responding to a reviewer on his ostinato-based tunes, Tolliver credits Jackie McLean's debut date and Andrew Hill for that approach.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: I do. I think that’s why Ellington kept his band together for so long, right? That is an interesting observation. I had a quote here about both your composing and your playing. It comes from one of those Jazz on CD books. And this particular reviewer made the observation that most of your compositions instead of complex chords, I think he’s referring to like bebop, “Charles favors basic motifs, four or five notes in an ostinato,” and then he continued, “it’s very much harder to play inventively over such a background where other chords offer endless permutations of changes. But Tolliver develops solo material apparently without limit in a highly lyrical mainstream style that recalls Clifford Brown.” So I think the gist of that is he’s pointing out that harmonically your music was simplified from some of those complex fast changes in the bebop world, but you still managed to find ways to solo over that.

Well you know I wouldn’t be where I am today, you know, in this art form, had it not been for Jackie McLean. That’s what I’m talking about, that lucky break you know. And my first, my debut recording with him, as you know, Jackie was a dye-in-the-wool, you know, bebopper. But that was, I came in during that generational shift just as you know the freer forms were being used. I mean he was already, he had already done “Destination Out” and a couple of other things which portend that he, you know, he wasn’t just sitting doing bebop endlessly. And my debut recording with him I mean you know us kids at the time we ate and slept Jackie McLean and all those guys. So we had it down, the bebop

thing. And he wanted something a little bit different. And so you know like half of that recording is bebop and half of it is what you are talking about. And from that experience I think is where I started to do those sorts of things that this person observed in my work. But I think Andrew Hill is the one who really, once I started playing with Andrew and recording with him, you know, that sort of thing really became also a part of my delivery process.
